'''''Equisetum telmateia''''', the '''great horsetail''', is a species of ''[[Equisetum]]'' (horsetail) [[Native species|native]] to [[Europe]], western [[Asia]] and northwest [[Africa]].<ref name="Hyde-1978">Hyde, H. A., Wade, A. E., & Harrison, S. G. (1978). ''Welsh Ferns''. National Museum of Wales {{ISBN|0-7200-0210-9}}.</ref><ref name="BSBI Plant Atlas-2020">{{cite web |title=Great Horsetail ''Equisetum telmateia'' Ehrh. |work=BSBI Online Plant Atlas 2020 |editor1=P. A. Stroh |editor2=T. A. Humphrey |editor3=R. J. Burkmar |editor4=O. L. Pescott |editor5=D. B. Roy |editor6=K. J. Walker |publisher=Botanical Society of Britain and Ireland |date=2020 |url=https://plantatlas2020.org/atlas/2cd4p9h.4k3 |access-date=16 September 2024 }}</ref> It was formerly widely treated in a broader sense including a [[subspecies]] (subsp. ''braunii'') in western North America, but this is now treated as a separate species, ''[[Equisetum braunii]]''.<ref name="POWO-1">{{cite web |title=''Equisetum telmateia'' Ehrh. |work=Plants of the World Online |publisher=Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew|url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn%3Alsid%3Aipni.org%3Anames%3A20007435-1 |access-date=2024-09-16 }}</ref><ref name="POWO-2">{{cite web |title=''Equisetum braunii'' Milde |work=Plants of the World Online |publisher=Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew|url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:77178330-1 |access-date=2024-09-16 }}</ref>

==Description==
[[File:Equisetum telmateia, Ormskirk, Lancashire 2.jpg|thumb|left|Sterile (foliage) stems in late May at [[Ormskirk]], Lancashire, UK]]
It is a [[herbaceous]] [[perennial plant]], with separate green [[photosynthesis|photosynthetic]] sterile stems, and pale yellowish non-photosynthetic [[spore]]-bearing fertile stems. The sterile stems, produced in late spring and dying down in late autumn, are {{convert|30|–|150|cm|abbr=on}} (rarely to {{convert|240|cm|abbr=on}}) tall (the tallest species of horsetail outside of tropical regions) and {{convert|1|cm|abbr=on}} diameter, heavily branched, with whorls of 14–40 branches, these up to {{convert|20|cm|abbr=on}} long, {{convert|1|–|2|mm|abbr=on|frac=64}} diameter and unbranched, emerging from the axils of a ring of [[bract]]s; the main stem itself is whitish, without chlorophyll or stomata. The fertile stems are produced in early spring before the sterile shoots, growing to {{convert|15|–|45|cm|abbr=on}} tall with an apical spore-bearing [[strobilus]] {{convert|4|–|10|cm|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|1|–|2|cm|abbr=on}} broad, and no side branches. The spores disperse in mid spring, with the fertile stems dying immediately after spore release. It also spreads by means of rhizomes that have been observed to penetrate {{convert|4|m}} into wet clay soil, spreading laterally in multiple layers.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www2.fiu.edu/~chusb001/GiantEquisetum/Ecophysiology.html#RhizArch |title=Ecology and Physiology of the Giant Horsetails |access-date=2011-05-12 |archive-date=2011-07-21 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110721175904/http://www2.fiu.edu/~chusb001/GiantEquisetum/Ecophysiology.html#RhizArch }}</ref> Occasionally plants produce stems that are both fertile and photosynthetic.<ref name="Hyde-1978"/><ref name="CTW-1981">{{cite book|author1=Clapham, A. R. |author2=Tutin, T. G. |author3= Warburg, E. F. |name-list-style=amp |year=1981 | title=Excursion Flora of the British Isles | edition=3rd | location=Cambridge | publisher=[[Cambridge University Press|University Press]] | page=6 | isbn=0-521-23290-2}}</ref>

==Distribution==
Great horsetail is widespread across most of Europe north to 56° to 58° N.<ref name="Fitter-1984">{{cite book |last1=Fitter |first1=Richard |last2=Fitter |first2=Alastair |last3=Farrer |first3=Anne |title=Collins Guide to the Grasses, Sedges, Rushes and Ferns of Britain and Northern Europe |date=1984 |publisher=Collins |location=London |isbn=0-00-219136-9 |pages=188–191}}</ref> In [[Ireland]] and [[Great Britain]], it is widespread and often common in suitable habitats, but scarcer in [[Scotland]], particularly north of the [[Central Belt]], except for a notable concentration on [[Skye]]; the northernmost population of the species anywhere is near [[Thurso]] on the north coast of Scotland at about 58°35' N.<ref name="BSBI Plant Atlas-2020"/> Further east, it does not reach so far north; in [[Sweden]], it is rare and endangered, confined to just three locations north to about 56°08' N on the west coast of the southern province of [[Skåne]].<ref name="Mattiasson-2000">{{cite journal |last1=Mattiasson |first1=Göran |title=Jättefräken — utveckling och tillbakagång |journal=Svensk Botanisk Tidskrift |date=2000 |volume=94 |issue=1 |pages=53–55 |url=http://uu.diva-portal.org/smash/get/diva2:1203055/FULLTEXT01 |access-date=17 September 2024 |language=Swedish}}</ref> Its southern and eastern limits are less well mapped, but it occurs south to [[Madeira]] (32°45' N), the [[Atlas Mountains]] in northwest Africa, and [[Israel]], and east to [[Iran]];<ref name="POWO-1"/> the easternmost mapped on [[iNaturalist]] ('research grade' records only) is at 52°58' E in Iran.<ref name="iNaturalist">{{cite web |title=Great Horsetail (''Equisetum telmateia'') |url=https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?verifiable=true&taxon_id=57030 |website=iNaturalist |access-date=17 September 2024}}</ref>

==Habitat==
It is found in damp shady places, spring [[fen]]s and [[seepage]] lines, usually in open woodlands, commonly forming large [[clonal colony|clonal colonies]].<ref name="BSBI Plant Atlas-2020"/><ref name="Hyde-1978"/><ref name="CTW-1981"/>
